prompt: In October 2026, what percent of U.S. registered voters had a favorable opinion of Elon Musk?
explanation: 39% of registered voters had a very or somewhat favorable opinion of Musk in the October 10–12, 2026 Economist/YouGov poll, more than for Mark Zuckerberg (25%). Opinion is almost entirely partisan: Civiqs' tracker of registered voters (Nov 18, 2026) had him at 37% favorable and 55% unfavorable, with 81% of Republicans and 3% of Democrats favorable.

source.title: Steady midterms picture, economic doubts, death penalty, and more: October 10–12, 2026 Economist/YouGov Poll

caveat: Favorability, not job approval. Both polls report this among registered voters (YouGov includes adult citizens who plan to register before Election Day), not all adults; the margin of error is about ±3.5 points.

prompt: In 2025, what share of Democrats (including independents who lean Democratic) said eating meat is either morally acceptable or not a moral issue at all?
explanation: 94% of Democrats and Democratic leaners say eating meat is morally acceptable (38%) or not a moral issue (56%); only 6% call it morally wrong. Republicans are at 98%. Of 15 behaviors Pew asked about, eating meat was the one fewest Americans called immoral (4%).

source.title: What Do Americans Consider Immoral? (Appendix: Detailed tables)

caveat: Party figures include leaners; Pew did not publish a liberal/conservative split for this item.

prompt: In 2026, rank these institutions by the share of U.S. adults who have 'a great deal' or 'quite a lot' of confidence in them.
explanation: Small business (67%) has topped the military (61%) every year since 2022. Congress is last of 17 institutions at 9%. Party gaps are large: 88% of Republicans vs. 42% of Democrats are confident in the military, and 50% of Democrats vs. 23% of Republicans in higher education.

source.title: Gallup News Service, June Wave 1 final topline: Confidence in Institutions

caveat: Telephone poll of 1,001 adults, margin of error ±4 points.

prompt: In 2025, what percent of Democrats (including independents who lean Democratic) said that being extremely rich, for example having billions of dollars, is morally wrong?
explanation: 29% of Democrats and leaners call it morally wrong; 58% say it is not a moral issue and 13% say it is morally acceptable. Among Republicans and leaners, 7% say it is wrong. Overall, 18% of U.S. adults do.

source.title: What Do Americans Consider Immoral? (Appendix: Detailed tables)

caveat: Party figures include leaners. Fieldwork was May 2025; results were published March 2026.

prompt: In Pew's 2023–24 survey, what share of U.S. adults said they believe in God or a universal spirit?
explanation: 83% believe in God or a universal spirit, though only 54% say they are absolutely certain. 70% believe in an afterlife, and 52% believe in both heaven and hell. Yet 49% seldom or never attend religious services.

source.title: If the U.S. had 100 people: Charting Americans' religious beliefs and practices

caveat: From the 2023–24 Religious Landscape Study (36,908 adults). The wording includes 'or a universal spirit', which gives a higher figure than questions about God alone.

prompt: Gallup asks Americans, with no list of options, to name the most important problem facing the country. Rank these answers by how often they were given in September 2026.
rankLabel: Named most often → named least often
explanation: Government and poor leadership (30%) was named more than twice as often as the cost of living (13%). Immigration drew 10%, healthcare 3%, and crime, climate, abortion and guns 1% or less each. All economic answers combined came to 31%.

source.title: Gallup Poll Social Series: Governance, final topline (Most Important Problem)

caveat: Open-ended question; people can name more than one problem (answers total 133%). It measures what comes to mind first, not everything people care about.

prompt: In November 2026, what share of Republicans said federal government officials should be banned from trading stocks?
explanation: 66% of Republicans favor a ban, close to Democrats (73%) and independents (62%); 67% of all adults do. It is one of the few current issues with near-equal support in both parties. For contrast, in the same poll stricter gun laws drew 89% of Democrats and 27% of Republicans.

source.title: Whether Congress should investigate the Trump administration, Jensen Huang, and more: November 13–16, 2026 Economist/YouGov Poll

caveat: 1,628 U.S. adult citizens, margin of error about ±2.9 points.
